title: Hydro-kinematics and hydro-dynamics
summary: Continuity, Bernoulli and momentum are the three conservation statements, and nearly every question is an application of one of them. The most examined single item is Bernoulli's list of assumptions, because a question will state one that has been violated. The dimensionless numbers are the other reliable source of marks: know which force ratio each represents and which class of flow it governs — Reynolds for pipes, Froude for open channels, Mach for compressible flow.

sections.heading: Describing flow — kinematics
sections.body:
**Classification of flow**, and each pair is a possible question:

| Pair | Distinction |
|---|---|
| **Steady / unsteady** | Whether properties at a **point** change with **time** |
| **Uniform / non-uniform** | Whether properties change with **position** along the flow |
| **Laminar / turbulent** | Orderly layers, or random mixing |
| **Compressible / incompressible** | Whether density changes |
| **Rotational / irrotational** | Whether fluid elements rotate about their own axes |
| One-, two-, three-dimensional | How many coordinates the velocity depends on |

The **steady/uniform** distinction is the one most often muddled: **steady** is about **time**, **uniform** about **space**. Flow through a converging pipe at constant discharge is **steady but non-uniform**; flow through a long straight pipe at a changing rate is **unsteady but uniform**.

**Flow lines:**

| Line | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Streamline** | A line everywhere **tangent to the velocity** — no flow crosses it |
| **Path line** | The **actual path** traced by one fluid particle over time |
| **Streak line** | The locus of particles that passed through one point |
| **Stream tube** | A tube bounded by streamlines |

In **steady** flow all three coincide, which is why the distinction only matters for unsteady flow.

**Continuity** — conservation of mass:

> **ρ₁A₁V₁ = ρ₂A₂V₂**,  and for incompressible flow **A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ = Q**

In differential form, for incompressible flow:

> **∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y + ∂w/∂z = 0**

That equation is the standard test of whether a given velocity field is **physically possible** — a favourite examination task. A field failing it violates conservation of mass and cannot exist.

**Velocity potential and stream function.** A **velocity potential φ** exists only for **irrotational** flow, with u = ∂φ/∂x. A **stream function ψ** exists for any **two-dimensional incompressible** flow, with u = ∂ψ/∂y and v = −∂ψ/∂x. Both satisfy the **Laplace equation** for irrotational incompressible flow, and **lines of constant φ and constant ψ are orthogonal** — which is exactly the property that makes a **flow net** work, whether for seepage under a dam or for flow around a body.

**Acceleration** has two parts, and forgetting the second is a classic error:

> **a = ∂V/∂t** (local, temporal) **+ V ∂V/∂s** (convective)

In **steady** flow the local term vanishes, but the **convective** term does not: a fluid particle passing through a nozzle accelerates even though nothing changes with time.

sections.heading: Bernoulli's equation and its applications
sections.body:
> **p/ρg + V²/2g + z = constant along a streamline**

The three terms are **pressure head**, **velocity head** and **datum (elevation) head**, all with units of length, and their sum is the **total head**.

**The assumptions — the single most examined item in the subchapter.** Bernoulli's equation requires the flow to be:

1. **Steady**
2. **Incompressible**
3. **Inviscid (frictionless)** — no energy loss
4. **Irrotational**, or applied **along a single streamline**
5. With **no energy added or removed** (no pump, no turbine)

A question will state a situation violating one of these and ask whether Bernoulli applies. The commonest violations in practice are **friction** (real pipes) and **energy addition** (a pump), both handled by extending the equation:

> **p₁/γ + V₁²/2g + z₁ + h_pump = p₂/γ + V₂²/2g + z₂ + h_turbine + h_loss**

**The two grade lines** follow directly:

| Line | Equals |
|---|---|
| **Hydraulic grade line (HGL)** | pressure head + datum head |
| **Total energy line (TEL)** | HGL + **velocity head** |

**TEL always falls** in the direction of flow (energy is always lost), but **HGL can rise** — at an expansion, where velocity head converts back to pressure head. And where the **HGL falls below the pipe**, the pressure is **negative**: a siphon operates there, and cavitation is a risk. Those three statements answer most HGL/TEL questions.

**Flow measurement devices** are all applications of Bernoulli plus continuity:

| Device | Coefficient of discharge |
|---|---|
| **Venturimeter** | **≈ 0.98** |
| **Orifice meter** | **≈ 0.62** |
| Nozzle meter | ≈ 0.95 |
| **Pitot tube** | ≈ 0.98 (velocity coefficient) |
| Rotameter, bend meter | — |

The **venturimeter's much higher C_d** is because its **gradual downstream expansion** recovers most of the pressure, whereas an orifice plate loses it in eddies. That is also why the venturimeter costs more and needs more length. Both work on the same principle: a **contraction raises velocity and lowers pressure**, and the measured pressure difference gives the discharge:

> **Q = C_d · (A₁A₂/√(A₁² − A₂²)) · √(2gh)**

**Orifice coefficients**, and their relationship:

> **C_d = C_c × C_v**

| Coefficient | Typical | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **C_c** coefficient of contraction | **0.62** | Area of the **vena contracta** ÷ orifice area |
| **C_v** coefficient of velocity | **0.98** | Actual velocity ÷ theoretical |
| **C_d** coefficient of discharge | **0.61** | Their product |

The **vena contracta** — the narrowest section of the jet, about half a diameter downstream — exists because the streamlines cannot turn a sharp corner instantly.

**A Pitot tube** measures the **stagnation** pressure, and the difference from the static pressure gives the velocity:

> **V = C_v √(2gh)**

It measures a **point** velocity, which is why a **Pitot-static tube traverse** is needed to obtain the mean velocity across a duct.

sections.heading: The momentum equation
sections.body:
> **ΣF = ρQ(V₂ − V₁)**

The **impulse–momentum principle** applied to a control volume. Its great advantage over Bernoulli is that it **does not require the flow to be frictionless** — it holds even where energy is lost, because momentum is conserved regardless. That makes it the tool for the **hydraulic jump**, sudden expansions, and any problem involving forces.

**Standard results, worth memorising:**

| Situation | Force |
|---|---|
| Jet on a **fixed flat plate, normal** | **F = ρAV²** |
| Jet on a fixed plate inclined at θ | F = ρAV² sin θ (normal to plate) |
| Jet on a **fixed curved vane, turned through 180°** | **F = 2ρAV²** |
| Jet on a **moving** flat plate (velocity u) | F = ρA(V − u)² |
| Jet on a moving curved vane, 180° | F = 2ρA(V − u)² |

The **factor of two** for a 180° vane is the whole reason a **Pelton bucket is split and turns the jet nearly back on itself**: reversing the momentum extracts twice the force of merely stopping it. In practice the deflection is about 165° rather than 180°, so the returning jet does not strike the following bucket.

**Work done and efficiency** for a jet on a moving vane: the work rate is F × u, which is zero at u = 0 (no movement) and zero at u = V (no relative velocity), so it has a **maximum in between**. Differentiating gives:

> **Maximum efficiency at u = V/2** for a flat plate and for a **Pelton wheel**

This is the key result of impulse turbine theory, and it is derived rather than assumed.

**Forces on bends and nozzles** are the standard practical application. For a bend, resolve the momentum equation in two directions, including the **pressure forces** on the inlet and outlet faces:

> **F_x = p₁A₁ − p₂A₂cos θ − ρQ(V₂cos θ − V₁)**

The resultant is what an **anchor block** must resist — which is why penstock anchor blocks are placed at every change of direction, and why their design combines momentum change, internal pressure and the weight component along the slope.

**Sudden expansion** is the classic case where momentum succeeds and Bernoulli fails, because the energy loss is unknown in advance. Applying momentum across the expansion yields the loss:

> **h_L = (V₁ − V₂)²/2g**

which could not have been obtained from the energy equation alone. Borda–Carnot's result, and a good illustration of when to reach for which tool.

sections.heading: Dimensional analysis and similitude
sections.body:
**Why it exists.** A full-scale hydraulic structure cannot be tested, so a **model** must be built — and the results are only transferable if the model and prototype are **similar** in the right sense. Dimensional analysis identifies which quantity must be matched.

**Three kinds of similarity**, all required:

| Similarity | Requires |
|---|---|
| **Geometric** | Same **shape** — all length ratios equal |
| **Kinematic** | Same **velocity** pattern — all velocity ratios equal |
| **Dynamic** | Same **force** ratios — the dimensionless numbers equal |

**The dimensionless numbers**, each a ratio of inertial force to one other force:

| Number | Ratio | Governs | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Reynolds Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν** | Inertia / **viscous** | Viscous flows | **Pipe flow**, submerged bodies, laminar–turbulent transition |
| **Froude Fr = V/√(gL)** | Inertia / **gravity** | Free-surface flows | **Open channels**, spillways, weirs, ships, hydraulic jumps |
| **Euler Eu = V/√(p/ρ)** | Inertia / **pressure** | Pressure-driven flow | Cavitation |
| **Weber We = ρV²L/σ** | Inertia / **surface tension** | Very small scales | Droplets, capillary waves, thin films |
| **Mach M = V/c** | Inertia / **elastic** | **Compressible** flow | High-speed gas flow, water hammer |

**Choosing which to match** is the practical question, and it is decided by **which force dominates**:

| Problem | Match |
|---|---|
| Flow in a **closed pipe** | **Reynolds** |
| A **spillway, weir, channel or river model** | **Froude** — gravity dominates a free surface |
| Drag on a fully submerged body | Reynolds |
| A ship (has both a free surface and viscous drag) | Both — impossible, so **Froude** is matched and the viscous part is corrected separately |

That last row is worth noting: **Reynolds and Froude cannot generally be satisfied simultaneously** in a scale model, which is why ship testing separates the wave-making resistance (Froude-scaled) from the frictional resistance (calculated).

**Transition values to memorise:**

| Flow | Laminar | Transitional | Turbulent |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pipe** (using D) | **Re < 2000** | 2000 – 4000 | **Re > 4000** |
| **Open channel** (using R) | Re < 500 | 500 – 2000 | > 2000 |
| Flat plate boundary layer | Re < 5 × 10⁵ | — | > 5 × 10⁵ |

**Froude number and open-channel regime:**

| Fr | Regime | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **< 1** | **Subcritical** | Deep, slow; disturbances travel **upstream** |
| **= 1** | **Critical** | Minimum specific energy |
| **> 1** | **Supercritical** | Shallow, fast; disturbances **cannot** travel upstream |

The upstream-propagation criterion is the physical meaning: Fr = 1 is where the flow velocity equals the speed of a surface wave, √(gy). That is why a hydraulic jump forms only in supercritical flow, and why upstream conditions control subcritical flow while downstream conditions cannot.

**Buckingham's π theorem** is the formal method: with **n variables** and **m fundamental dimensions**, there are **(n − m)** independent dimensionless groups. Choosing **repeating variables** that together contain all the dimensions — typically a length, a velocity and a density — produces the standard numbers above.

**Model scales** are commonly **distorted** for rivers, where a geometrically similar model would be too shallow for measurable flow: the vertical scale is exaggerated relative to the horizontal. The distortion must be reported, because it changes the slope and hence the friction relationships.

formulas.label: Continuity
formulas.note: The differential form is the standard test of whether a velocity field is physically possible.

formulas.label: Bernoulli's equation (extended)
formulas.expression: p₁/γ + V₁²/2g + z₁ + h_pump = p₂/γ + V₂²/2g + z₂ + h_turbine + h_loss
formulas.note: Assumes steady, incompressible, inviscid, irrotational flow along a streamline.

formulas.label: Venturimeter / orifice meter discharge
formulas.note: C_d ≈ 0.98 venturimeter, 0.62 orifice meter — the venturi recovers pressure in its gradual expansion.

formulas.label: Orifice coefficients
formulas.note: C_c relates to the vena contracta, about half a diameter downstream of the orifice.

formulas.label: Momentum equation
formulas.note: Valid even where energy is lost, unlike Bernoulli — hence its use for the hydraulic jump.

formulas.label: Force of a jet
formulas.expression: flat plate F = ρAV² ;   180° curved vane F = 2ρAV² ;   moving vane use (V − u)
formulas.note: Maximum work at u = V/2 — the basis of Pelton wheel design.

formulas.label: Sudden expansion loss
formulas.note: Obtained from the MOMENTUM equation; the energy equation alone cannot give it.

formulas.label: Dimensionless numbers
formulas.expression: Re = VD/ν (viscous) ;  Fr = V/√(gL) (gravity) ;  M = V/c (elastic) ;  We = ρV²L/σ (surface tension)
formulas.note: Match Reynolds for pipes, Froude for free-surface flows. Both cannot generally be matched at once.

formulas.label: Buckingham's π theorem
formulas.expression: number of dimensionless groups = n − m     (n variables, m fundamental dimensions)
formulas.note: Repeating variables are chosen to contain all the dimensions — typically a length, a velocity and a density.
